Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Public access faces navigation and social space; service access faces the alley, utility corridor, backstage zone, waterfront service edge, or maintenance route. Foundation, stairs, ramps, porches, piles, retaining walls, and terrain transitions must meet the environment without floating gaps. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Expected hooks include changeable display, content, or emissive state. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use modular floor, wall, roof, stair, rail, counter, doorway, foundation, and major structural collision. Walkable areas, entrances, windows used for gameplay, and service openings must match the visible model, while trim, roof equipment, cables, fasteners, and inaccessible facade detail remain simplified or nonblocking. Use positive Z as the principal entrance, public face, or module-forward direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at ground level or the documented connection plane near the footprint center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Preserve massing, entrances, openings, supports, and skyline in every LOD. Medium-range output should target roughly 18,000 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 6,000 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Establish the building or structural-module category from massing, roof or overhead profile, entrance or connection hierarchy, structural bays, openings, and ground or support relationship before signage and color are visible.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

Keep the item queued as unsupported until a purpose-built family generator exists. The object must remain immediately recognizable from silhouette and required components, use physically coherent construction and human or vehicle scale, and follow the town direction: dense entertainment district realism; layered signage, hotel facades, service infrastructure, parking, backstage logistics, controlled spectacle. This asset appears under the blueprint section “E. Hotel/hospitality” and should visibly support that gameplay or environmental role rather than acting as generic filler. The blueprint evidence is: B. Strip roads/street props C. Game hall D. Arcade E. Hotel/hospitality

Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is vehicle because whole physical-object token resolves the asset as vehicle. Model it as a mechanically plausible transportation asset whose occupancy, cargo, propulsion, cooling, lighting, access, protection, and service systems are visually understandable. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: The transportation class must read from front, side, rear, and three-quarter views through stance, cabin or operator placement, overhangs, propulsion spacing, body volumes, glazing, and travel direction before decals or glow are considered. Keep the working envelope near 1.5 meters wide, 1.5 meters deep, and 1.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Hotel Bell Cart; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Include a load-bearing chassis or hull, occupant or cargo volume, access, controls, lighting, propulsion hardware, cooling or intake paths, service panels, energy connection, protected underside, and environment-specific safety systems. Required visible components are recognizable primary structure, functional secondary components, appropriate materials. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary architectural metal, glass, controlled illuminated trim, service-grade structure, violet, electric blue, warm gold, red, black, cream. dense entertainment district realism; layered signage, hotel facades, service infrastructure, parking, backstage logistics, controlled spectacle. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: flat billboard walls, single-casino emptiness, unreadable rainbow clutter. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Apply restrained lived-in wear at contact points, lower edges, hinges, handles, feet, fasteners, drainage paths, service openings, tires, exposed corners, or frequently cleaned surfaces. Match the district’s maintenance level rather than using uniform dirt or uniform perfection. Spawn it on a road, parking bay, rail, waterline, dock, garage, flight socket, or hover pad appropriate to the propulsion system. Preserve forward direction, idle stance, occupant entry, cargo or passenger clearance, turning or docking envelope, camera framing, and surrounding safety space. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Keep access panels, doors, lights, propulsion units, controls, cargo areas, steering surfaces, lift hardware, and service interfaces separately named for animation, customization, damage, maintenance, and gameplay states. Expected hooks include transform, material-state, damage, pickup, or placement hook only where gameplay requires it. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use a stable chassis or hull collider with optional cabin, cargo, propulsion, or hit-region hulls. Do not trace every light, mirror, vent, wheel, pod, railing, rope, or fastener. Entry sockets and clearance volumes must align with the visible body. Use positive Z as forward and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground, waterline, rail, or hover-plane center below the chassis or hull, with separate transforms for propulsion and steering hardware. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use sufficient geometry for reflective silhouette surfaces while economizing hidden undersides. Reuse repeated seats, lights, vents, wheels, pods, rails, and fasteners. LODs must preserve occupancy and propulsion logic. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 23,400 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 10,800 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 3,600 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: The transportation class must read from front, side, rear, and three-quarter views through stance, cabin or operator placement, overhangs, propulsion spacing, body volumes, glazing, and travel direction before decals or glow are considered.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Hotel Bell Cart is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.
